Introduction

introduction.Rmd

nomad stores fitted mobility models for infectious disease modelling. The usual workflow is:

  1. identify a plausible source mobility dataset;
  2. inspect the fitted models available for that dataset;
  3. prepare a distance matrix and population vector for the prediction setting;
  4. predict a mobility matrix;
  5. check warnings and sensitivity to alternative models.
library(nomad)

Available Data And Models

The mobility catalogue describes the datasets used to fit the models in the package. Looking through it helps us find data collected in settings similar to our own, taking account of when movement was measured, whose journeys were recorded and the size of the regions. These details will help us decide which models are worth exploring for our analysis.

mobility_table()

Some datasets are included in the catalogue because they may be useful for future analyses, although we do not yet have their fitted models. The has_fitted_models column lets us identify which datasets already have models that we can use. We can then look at the model catalogue to see the available variants and how well each fit the source data. For example, the following returns all the models fit to data from Zambia.

model_table(country = "ZMB")

Inspect A Model

Let’s choose the normalised exponential gravity model fit to the newer Zambia Facebook data. We can use model_profile() to see the number of source regions, their populations and distances, and the period represented by a prediction. This gives us a starting point for comparing the source setting with our own.

model <- model_db$zmb_fb_2025_mod_grav_exp_norm
model_profile(model)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 27
#>   name  data_name country aggregation date_start date_end   source_duration_days
#>   <chr> <chr>     <chr>   <chr>       <date>     <date>                    <dbl>
#> 1 zmb_… zmb_fb_2… ZMB     admin_2     2024-07-29 2025-06-16                   21
#> # ℹ 20 more variables: prediction_period_days <dbl>, distance_unit <chr>,
#> #   supports_newdata <lgl>, supports_stochastic_draws <lgl>, n_origin <int>,
#> #   n_dest <int>, distance_min <dbl>, distance_q25 <dbl>,
#> #   distance_median <dbl>, distance_q75 <dbl>, distance_max <dbl>,
#> #   population_total <dbl>, population_min <dbl>, population_median <dbl>,
#> #   population_max <dbl>, max_rhat <dbl>, min_n_eff <dbl>,
#> #   rhat_above_1_1 <lgl>, has_mobility_data <lgl>, has_saved_check <lgl>

We can then look at how well the model reproduced the observed trips using check() and plot(). These saved summaries are included even when the underlying trip observations cannot be shared publicly. The model selection vignette explains how to interpret them.

check(model, plots = FALSE)
#> $DIC
#> [1] NA
#> 
#> $RMSE
#> [1] 965441.9
#> 
#> $MAPE
#> [1] 32.18002
#> 
#> $R2
#> [1] 0.1056686
plot(model)

Prepare A Small Prediction Setting

To predict movement, we need a distance matrix D and a population vector N for our regions. These are the same inputs used by mobility::predict(). If the origins and destinations have different populations, they can instead be supplied as N_orig and N_dest.

Here we construct a small example with five place names. The populations and coordinates are invented to show how to arrange the inputs, and should not be used as estimates for those places. We multiply the distances between the coordinates by 120 to give our example distances in kilometres. For your own analysis, you could prepare these inputs from a shapefile and population data, as shown in the README example.

Show how to construct the example regions 
places <- data.frame(
  name = c("Lusaka", "Kabwe", "Ndola", "Kitwe", "Livingstone"),
  x = c(0, 1.2, 2.8, 2.6, -1.4),
  y = c(0, 1.0, 2.7, 2.4, -2.7),
  population = c(2500000, 230000, 475000, 690000, 170000)
)

D <- as.matrix(dist(places[, c("x", "y")])) * 120
dimnames(D) <- list(places$name, places$name)
N <- setNames(places$population, places$name)
newdata <- list(D = D, N = N)

Make A Prediction

We can now pass the distances and populations to predict(), specifying that our distances are in kilometres. You will see warnings because these five regions contain a smaller population and cover fewer locations than the data used to fit the model. The prediction can still be calculated, but those warnings help us identify differences between our example and the setting in which the model was fit.

M <- predict(model, newdata = newdata, unit = "km")
#> Warning: ! Prediction data have far fewer regions than the fitted source data.
#> ℹ `newdata` has "5" regions; the fitted model has "115".
#> • Predictions may be coarser than the source data can support.
#> Warning: ! Prediction population is much smaller than the fitted source population.
#> ℹ `newdata` population: "4065000"; fitted model source population: "18296043".
#> • Check that this model is suitable for the population scale being predicted.
round(M / 1000, 1)
#>              Lusaka  Kabwe  Ndola  Kitwe Livingstone
#> Lusaka      34681.3   53.7    0.0    0.0         0.1
#> Kabwe           4.9 3189.6    0.2    0.9         0.0
#> Ndola           0.0    0.3 5389.0 1210.3         0.0
#> Kitwe           0.0    2.1 1757.8 7826.9         0.0
#> Livingstone     0.0    0.0    0.0    0.0      2362.0
#> attr(,"model")
#> [1] "gravity"
#> attr(,"type")
#> [1] "exp_norm"
#> attr(,"source_duration_days")
#> [1] 21
#> attr(,"prediction_period_days")
#> [1] 21
#> attr(,"duration_scale")
#> [1] 1
#> attr(,"data_name")
#> [1] "zmb_fb_2025"

The result is a matrix in which rows identify the origin of a trip and columns identify its destination. We have divided the values by 1,000 to make them easier to read, so a value of 2 represents 2,000 predicted trips. These are counts of trips, to which a person may contribute more than once. The period is taken from the model metadata and is 21 days for this fit. The names on the distance matrix and population vector must identify the same regions so that nomad can match each population to the correct location.

For a real analysis, we would now consider whether the model describes movement at a suitable scale for our question. For example, a model fit to movement between districts may tell us little about journeys between neighbourhoods within a city. Comparing alternatives is useful when several models could plausibly describe the movement we want to study.

Predict for the source regions

The fitted model also includes the distances and populations used for fitting. These inputs are often called covariates. We can reuse them to predict movement for the original regions, which provides a useful comparison with predictions for a new setting.

source_data <- model$get_model()$data[c("D", "N_orig", "N_dest")]
M_source <- predict(model, newdata = source_data)
M_source[1:5, 1:5]
#>            destination
#> origin         ZMB.1.1_1    ZMB.1.2_1    ZMB.1.3_1    ZMB.1.4_1    ZMB.1.5_1
#>   ZMB.1.1_1 4.503207e+06 207404.91311 1.175758e+01 2.866407e+03 3.067882e+05
#>   ZMB.1.2_1 4.595483e+04 997777.28396 2.401973e+01 4.359945e+01 1.965902e+05
#>   ZMB.1.3_1 2.233465e+00     20.59288 8.554261e+05 1.436979e-03 3.196422e+01
#>   ZMB.1.4_1 8.675690e+02     59.55731 2.289578e-03 1.362974e+06 5.927834e+01
#>   ZMB.1.5_1 1.268509e+05 366863.60721 6.957575e+01 8.098131e+01 1.861987e+06

Choose a prediction period

If we want a prediction for a different time period, we can supply duration in days or a date_start/date_end pair. This scales the prediction in proportion to the period recorded in the model metadata, assuming that the average daily trip rate stays constant. For example, the request below uses 30 / 21 as its multiplier because the newer Facebook models predict trip counts over 21 days. The dates over which data were collected are stored separately and do not determine this multiplier.

M_30 <- predict(model, newdata = source_data, duration = 30)
attr(M_30, "duration_scale")
#> [1] 1.428571

The returned duration_scale is the multiplier applied to the original prediction, in this case approximately 1.43.

Models can also be shared through nomad with incomplete source metadata, as with the earlier Zambia Facebook and CDR models from 2020. Without a prediction period, we can explore their unscaled predictions but cannot convert the counts to trips over a specified number of days. The package warns when returning such a prediction and raises an error if we request a duration conversion. This makes the available models accessible while showing where missing information limits their use in an analysis.

Compare Alternatives

Several models were fit to the Zambia Facebook observations. We can compare their fit statistics and use model_weights() to calculate weights from one of those measures. Here we use root mean squared error (RMSE), which gives more weight to models that reproduced the source observations more closely. This comparison uses models fit to the same dataset, so their errors refer to the same observed trips.

weights <- model_weights(data_name = "zmb_fb_2025", metric = "RMSE")
weights[, c("name", "RMSE", "weight")]
#> # A tibble: 12 × 3
#>    name                                    RMSE   weight
#>    <chr>                                  <dbl>    <dbl>
#>  1 zmb_fb_2025_mod_dd_exp               946018. 0.0898  
#>  2 zmb_fb_2025_mod_dd_power             946521. 0.0897  
#>  3 zmb_fb_2025_mod_dd_radiation         946973. 0.0897  
#>  4 zmb_fb_2025_mod_grav_basic        819787890. 0.000104
#>  5 zmb_fb_2025_mod_grav_exp             947086. 0.0897  
#>  6 zmb_fb_2025_mod_grav_exp_norm        965442. 0.0879  
#>  7 zmb_fb_2025_mod_grav_power           942100. 0.0901  
#>  8 zmb_fb_2025_mod_grav_power_norm      946881. 0.0897  
#>  9 zmb_fb_2025_mod_grav_scaled_power    952655. 0.0891  
#> 10 zmb_fb_2025_mod_grav_transport      1057907. 0.0803  
#> 11 zmb_fb_2025_mod_rad_basic            831656. 0.102   
#> 12 zmb_fb_2025_mod_rad_finite           833482. 0.102

We can also use nomad_ensemble() to combine predictions from several models. For a simple example, we will select the exponential departure-diffusion model and combine it with the gravity model used above. Both were fit to the same Facebook dataset. Because we ask each model to predict for the same regions and period, we can take a weighted average of their predicted trip counts. We choose weights of 0.5 for this example, giving each model equal influence, rather than deriving the weights from their fit statistics.

departure_model <- model_db$zmb_fb_2025_mod_dd_exp
ensemble <- nomad_ensemble(
  list(departure = departure_model, gravity = model),
  weights = c(departure = 0.5, gravity = 0.5)
)
M_ensemble <- predict(ensemble, newdata = newdata, unit = "km")
#> Warning: ! Prediction data have far fewer regions than the fitted source data.
#> ℹ `newdata` has "5" regions; the fitted model has "115".
#> • Predictions may be coarser than the source data can support.
#> Warning: ! Prediction population is much smaller than the fitted source population.
#> ℹ `newdata` population: "4065000"; fitted model source population: "18296043".
#> • Check that this model is suitable for the population scale being predicted.
#> Warning: ! Prediction data have far fewer regions than the fitted source data.
#> ℹ `newdata` has "5" regions; the fitted model has "115".
#> • Predictions may be coarser than the source data can support.
#> Warning: ! Prediction population is much smaller than the fitted source population.
#> ℹ `newdata` population: "4065000"; fitted model source population: "18296043".
#> • Check that this model is suitable for the population scale being predicted.
round(sum(M_ensemble))
#> [1] 56989960

Explore parameter uncertainty

So far we have used the mean fitted parameters to make each prediction. Setting nsim to a value greater than one instead gives repeated predictions using approximate parameter draws from the stored means and standard deviations. The summary below reports how much the total number of trips and the number between different regions vary across those draws. This captures parameter uncertainty within the selected model, while comparing alternative models lets us explore uncertainty about the choice of model itself.

draws <- predict(model, newdata = source_data, nsim = 10, seed = 1)
uncertainty_summary(draws, metrics = c("total", "between_region"))
#> # A tibble: 6 × 3
#>   metric          prob      value
#>   <chr>          <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1 total          0.025 254163766.
#> 2 total          0.5   254206733.
#> 3 total          0.975 254234581.
#> 4 between_region 0.025  93395200.
#> 5 between_region 0.5    93420244.
#> 6 between_region 0.975  93436944.

To explore these choices further, Selecting a mobility model works through the warnings and uncertainty summaries in more detail, and shows how to compare predictions from several models. Once you have a set of plausible models, Identifying a mobility model for an outbreak shows how to compare them using the daily incidence of a simulated outbreak.
